title: Keep the Cards
bodyMd:
This is an argumentative passage. Three places are marked with a bracketed number and shown in **bold**. The sentences of paragraph 3 are numbered so that a question can refer to them.

**Paragraph 1.** When the Ridgeway Public Library finished moving its catalog online, the oak cabinet in the lobby lost its official purpose. The board voted to keep it anyway. **[1] The library's director, Feliks Adamou insisted** on that vote, and three years later it looks less sentimental than it did at the time.

**Paragraph 2.** The cabinet earns its floor space by doing something a search box cannot. A reader who types in a title gets that title. A reader who opens a drawer gets that title and every card filed on either side of it. **[2] Neither the search box nor the drawers is complete on their own**, but only the drawers put a reader next to a book that nobody told her to look for.

**Paragraph 3.** **[3]** (1) The library's online records stop at 1974. (2) The cabinet, by contrast, holds a card for every book the library has ever owned. (3) Anything published before that year was never keyed in. (4) A reader looking for a book from 1910, then, has no choice but to open a drawer.

**Paragraph 4.** The cabinet is not free. It takes up about four square metres of a lobby the board could rent to the coffee counter next door, and a staff member spends an hour a month refiling cards that visitors pull out and push back carelessly. The board reviews the arrangement every year, and every year it has voted the same way.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph argumentative passage arguing that the invented Ridgeway Public Library was right to keep its card catalog after moving its records online. Paragraph one reports the board's vote and names the director, Feliks Adamou. Paragraph two argues that a drawer lets a reader browse neighbouring cards in a way a search box does not. Paragraph three, whose four sentences are numbered, states that the online records stop at 1974, that the cabinet holds a card for every book ever owned, that anything published before 1974 was never keyed in, and that a reader wanting a book from 1910 must therefore open a drawer. Paragraph four acknowledges the floor space and staff time the cabinet costs. Three places are marked for editing. Marked place one, in paragraph one, is the phrase "The library's director, Feliks Adamou insisted". Marked place two, in paragraph two, is the clause "Neither the search box nor the drawers is complete on their own". Marked place three is the position at the start of paragraph three, before its numbered sentences.

provenance.notes: Original argumentative passage. The Ridgeway Public Library, Feliks Adamou, the 1974 cutoff and every figure are invented for this item set; nothing is taken from, or modelled on, a published ACT English passage.
